explanation: Web pages, images and scripts Chrome saved so pages load faster. Safe to clean. Chrome rebuilds it as you browse, and you stay signed in to every site.
Chromium's copy of pages and images it has already downloaded. Safe to clean. It rebuilds as you browse and does not affect your logins or history.
Brave's saved copies of web content. Safe to clean. Nothing about your logins, bookmarks or history is touched.
Edge's saved copies of web content. Safe to clean. You stay signed in everywhere.
Vivaldi's saved copies of web content. Safe to clean, and your session is unaffected.
Opera's saved copies of web content. Safe to clean, and your session is unaffected.
Firefox's network cache: pages, images and scripts saved so sites load faster. Safe to clean. Your tabs, logins, bookmarks and history all live elsewhere and are not touched.
A precompiled copy of Firefox's own interface, kept to make it launch faster. Safe to clean. The next launch is slightly slower while it rebuilds.
Cached message bodies and images. Safe to clean. Your mail, accounts and local folders are untouched and re-download as you read.
Compiled JavaScript the browser keeps so pages start faster. Safe to clean and rebuilt automatically.
Compiled graphics shaders the browser reuses to draw pages. Safe to clean. It is rebuilt the next time you open the browser.
Files websites stored so they work offline or load instantly. Safe to clean. Sites re-download them on your next visit and you stay signed in.
The local list of known-dangerous sites. Safe to clean. The browser downloads a fresh copy automatically.
Small preview images the file manager generated for your photos and videos. Safe to clean. They regenerate as you browse folders.
An index of the fonts installed on this machine. Safe to clean and rebuilt automatically the next time an app loads fonts.
Compiled graphics shaders your GPU driver keeps so games and apps start faster. Safe to clean. The first launch after cleaning is slower while it rebuilds.
GNOME's index of your files, used by search. Deleting it is safe, but search results are incomplete until it finishes rebuilding, which can take a while.
App listings and screenshots the Software app downloaded. Safe to clean and re-fetched on next open.
Temporary data for an app installed through Flatpak. Safe to clean. The app rebuilds whatever it still needs.
Temporary data for an app installed through Snap. Safe to clean. The app rebuilds whatever it still needs.
Temporary web content stored by a desktop app built on Electron. Safe to clean. The app re-downloads what it needs and you stay signed in.
Files you have already deleted but not yet permanently removed. Emptying the trash frees this space, but anything in it is gone for good.
Diagnostic logs written by apps. Safe to clean unless you are in the middle of debugging something.
Packages npm has already downloaded, kept so future installs are faster. Safe to clean. npm re-downloads what a project needs on the next install.
Throwaway packages npx downloaded to run a one-off command. Safe to clean.
Packages Yarn has downloaded. Safe to clean. Yarn re-downloads them on the next install.
pnpm's shared package store. Safe to clean, though every project using pnpm will re-download its dependencies on the next install.
Packages Bun has downloaded. Safe to clean and refetched on the next install.
Modules Deno downloaded and compiled. Safe to clean. Deno refetches them the next time you run a script.
Node header files kept for building native modules. Safe to clean and re-downloaded when needed.
Electron binaries downloaded while building desktop apps. Safe to clean. They are re-downloaded on the next build.
Node versions nvm downloaded. Safe to clean; installed Node versions themselves are kept.
Type definitions TypeScript cached for editor autocomplete. Safe to clean and rebuilt automatically.
Browser builds Playwright downloaded for automated testing. Safe to clean. Running a test again downloads them back, which takes a few minutes.
Chromium builds Puppeteer downloaded for automated testing. Safe to clean and re-downloaded when a test runs.
Cypress test runner binaries. Safe to clean. The next test run downloads the version it needs.
Python packages pip has already downloaded. Safe to clean. pip re-downloads what you install next.
Python packages uv has downloaded. Safe to clean and refetched on the next install.
Packages and metadata Poetry downloaded. Safe to clean. Poetry refetches on the next install.
Packages Pipenv downloaded. Safe to clean and refetched on the next install.
Virtual environments Pipenv created for your projects. Deleting them is safe but each project needs pipenv install again before it runs.
Hook environments pre-commit built for your repos. Safe to clean; they rebuild the next time hooks run.
Packages conda downloaded and unpacked. Deleting them is safe, but rebuilding an environment means downloading several gigabytes again.

The Dart SDK, engine binaries and platform artifacts Flutter downloaded into its own install folder. Deleting it is safe, but the next flutter command re-downloads one to two gigabytes before it can build.
Dart and Flutter packages downloaded by pub. Safe to clean. Running flutter pub get or dart pub get restores whatever a project needs.
Small settings and state files the Flutter tool keeps between runs. Safe to clean and rebuilt on the next command.
Generated files Dart and Flutter builds keep inside a project. Safe to clean. They regenerate on the next build.
Dependencies and build outputs Gradle keeps so builds are faster. Safe to clean. The next build re-downloads what it needs, which takes longer than usual once.
Logs from Gradle's background build process. Safe to clean.
Full copies of Gradle, one per version any project has ever asked for. Deleting them is safe, but the next build of each project downloads its version again.
System images used to run Android emulators. Deleting them is safe, but each one is several gigabytes to download again, and an emulator using a deleted image will not start until you reinstall it.
Native development kits, around three gigabytes per version. Deleting older versions is safe, but a project pinned to one will need to download it again.
SDK platform files for older Android API levels. Deleting them is safe unless a project still targets that level, in which case Android Studio re-downloads it.
Superseded versions of the Android build tools. Deleting them is safe; the newest version is kept.
Partial downloads and unpacking leftovers from the Android SDK manager. Safe to clean.
Intermediate build output the Android tools keep between builds. Safe to clean and rebuilt on the next build.
Saved emulator states used for fast boot. Safe to clean. Your virtual devices and everything installed on them are kept; they just cold-boot next time.
Android Studio's indexes and caches for your projects. Deleting them is safe, but Studio re-indexes each project on the next open, which takes a few minutes.
Java dependencies Maven downloaded. Safe to clean. The next build re-downloads what each project needs.
Full copies of Maven downloaded by the wrapper. Deleting them is safe; each project re-downloads its version on the next build.
Compilers and libraries Kotlin/Native downloaded. Deleting them is safe, but the next build downloads several gigabytes again.
Java runtimes downloaded by your IDE or Gradle. Deleting them is safe unless a project is pinned to one, which then downloads again.
Scala and sbt dependencies downloaded by Coursier or Ivy. Safe to clean and re-downloaded on the next build.
Rust crates Cargo downloaded. Safe to clean. cargo build re-downloads what each project needs.
Installed Rust compiler versions. Deleting unused ones is safe, but each is a few hundred megabytes to reinstall. The active toolchain is kept.
Cached compiler output used to speed up rebuilds. Safe to clean; the next build is slower once.
Compiled Go packages kept to make builds faster. Safe to clean and rebuilt on the next build.
Go modules downloaded for your projects. Safe to clean. go build re-downloads what it needs.
Lint results cached between runs. Safe to clean.
Cached C and C++ compiler output. Safe to clean; the next full build is slower once.
Bazel's build output and downloaded dependencies. Safe to clean, though the next build is a full rebuild.
Compiled Zig artifacts. Safe to clean and rebuilt on the next build.
Gem files Ruby downloaded. Safe to clean; bundle install refetches them.
PHP packages Composer downloaded. Safe to clean and refetched on the next install.
.NET packages NuGet downloaded. Safe to clean. dotnet restore refetches what a project needs.
Provider plugins Terraform downloaded. Safe to clean; terraform init downloads them again.
Virtual machine images Vagrant downloaded. Deleting them is safe, but each box is a large download to restore.
Machine learning models and datasets downloaded from Hugging Face. Deleting them is safe, but these are large downloads to restore.
Unity's asset and package cache. Safe to clean; Unity rebuilds it on the next project open.

Space Docker reports it could reclaim from stopped containers, unused images and build cache. This app does not touch Docker's storage directly; run docker system prune yourself so the daemon stays consistent.
Cached extension downloads and workspace state for Visual Studio Code. Safe to clean. Editor settings, extensions and open folders are not affected.
Cached data and workspace state for Cursor. Safe to clean; your settings and extensions are kept.
Project indexes and caches for IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm and friends. Deleting them is safe, but each project re-indexes on the next open.
Copies of the VS Code server installed by Remote-SSH, one per version you have connected with. Deleting them is safe; the next remote connection reinstalls the current one.
Older copies of editor extensions left behind after updates. Safe to clean; only superseded versions are removed.
Cached data for the Zed editor. Safe to clean.
The dependencies installed for this project. Safe to remove; npm ci or your package manager reinstalls them from the lockfile.
Yarn's in-project package cache. Safe to remove; yarn install restores it.
Compiled output for this Rust project. Safe to remove; cargo build regenerates it, taking longer once.
The Python virtual environment for this project. Safe to remove; recreate it and reinstall from requirements.txt or pyproject.toml.
Bytecode and tool caches Python generated while running this project. Safe to remove and regenerated automatically.
Generated output from this project's last build. Safe to remove; rebuild regenerates it.
Build output and caches for this Gradle project. Safe to remove; the next build regenerates them.
PHP dependencies installed for this project. Safe to remove; composer install restores them.
Compiled output and fetched dependencies for this project. Safe to remove; mix deps.get and mix compile restore them.
Compiled output for this .NET project. Safe to remove; dotnet build regenerates it.
Gems installed into this project. Safe to remove; bundle install restores them.
Provider plugins and modules for this Terraform project. Safe to remove; terraform init restores them.
Compiled output from this project's last build. Safe to remove; rebuild regenerates it.
A language model you downloaded with Ollama. Deleting it frees a lot of space, but pulling it again is a large download.
A language model you downloaded in LM Studio. Deleting it frees a lot of space, but downloading it again takes a while.
A language model downloaded by GPT4All. Deleting it is safe but it is a large download to restore.
Installer files APT kept after installing or updating packages. Safe to clean. Your installed software is not affected; APT simply re-downloads a package if it ever needs to reinstall it.
The catalogue of packages available from your software sources. Deleting it is safe, but the next apt update has to download the full catalogue again.
Packages that were installed automatically as dependencies and nothing needs any more. Removing them is normally safe, but read the list first if you installed something by hand.

Older Linux kernel versions kept after updates. Removing them frees space in /boot, but keep at least one older kernel as a fallback in case the newest one fails to boot. The running kernel and the newest are always kept.
Configuration files left behind by packages you removed without purging. Removing them is safe unless you plan to reinstall one of those packages and want its old settings back.
The systemd journal, which grows over time. Trimming it to a size limit is safe; you keep recent logs and lose older entries.
Previous versions of your installed snaps, kept so you can roll back. Removing disabled revisions is safe; the current version of each snap stays installed.
Downloaded snap files kept after installation. Safe to clean.
Reports written when an app crashed. Safe to clean unless you are about to file a bug report.
Compressed older log files kept by log rotation. Safe to clean; current logs are untouched.
Flatpak runtimes no installed app depends on any more. Safe to remove; your apps keep the runtimes they actually use.
Settings and data left behind by an app that is no longer installed. Usually safe to remove, but check the name first in case you plan to reinstall it.
A cache folder an app created under ~/.cache. Anything here is temporary by definition and the app recreates whatever it still needs. Safe to clean.
Temporary files kept by an app installed through Flatpak. Safe to clean; the app rebuilds what it needs on the next launch.
Temporary files kept by an app installed through Snap. Safe to clean; the app rebuilds what it needs on the next launch.
A cache folder created by a developer tool. Safe to clean; the tool re-downloads or rebuilds what it needs on the next run.
